items.q: What does it mean to be saved by grace, and can I lose it?
a: Good question, and an honest one. Let me take the two halves separately.

Saved by grace means you did not earn it and cannot. Ephesians 2:8–9: salvation is a gift, not a result of works, so no one can boast. In your book's picture, a dead heart cannot perform CPR on itself. God gave the spark of new life (Titus 3:5). Your part is to receive it, then walk it out over a lifetime.

Can you lose it? Here is what I believe. Salvation is God's work, and He never takes it back. He wants everyone to be saved (1 Timothy 2:4), and Jesus said no one will snatch His sheep out of His hand (John 10:28). Hard seasons come to every believer, and stumbling is not losing. But a person who decides, knowingly, to renounce Christ can walk away from what God keeps offering. That is their choice, never God's. This is where the Assemblies of God and John Wesley stand too. Faithful believers see parts of it differently, and I won't argue with them.
What I want you to hear is this: salvation is the start. Sanctification is the lifelong walk of growing into Christlikeness.
Can I ask what is behind your question?
One step: read John 10:27–30 slowly this week and say it aloud as a prayer.
src: Spiritual Fitness: 6-Week Small Group Guide (Session 3)
8-Week Participant Workbook (Week 3)
30-Day Devotional (Days 14-15)

items.q: Do I have to do good works to be saved?
a: No. Works do not save you. They are what saved people do.

Ephesians 2:8–9 is plain: by grace you have been saved through faith, not from works. Then verse 10 turns the corner: we are God's workmanship, created in Christ Jesus for good works. The works come after the rescue, never before it.

In your book's picture: regeneration is the spark, one moment when God gives life. Sanctification is the marathon, a lifetime of walking with the Spirit. You do not train to get life. You train because you have it.
One step: ask yourself, "Am I serving to earn God's smile, or because I already have it?" Then do one small act of service for someone this week, from the second answer.
src: Spiritual Fitness: Master Bilingual Slides (Sermon 2)

items.q: What does repentance actually mean?
a: Repentance is more than feeling bad. The Greek word, metanoia, means a change of mind that turns into a change of direction.

When Jesus began to preach, He said, "Repent and believe the gospel" (Mark 1:15). To Nicodemus He said a person must be born again to see the kingdom (John 3:3–5), and He pointed to a child's trust as the way in (Matthew 18:1–4). In Acts 3:19, repenting and turning back comes with times of refreshing from the Lord. Notice that: repentance opens a door to refreshing. It is not a punishment.
If you are asking because you carry something, you do not have to carry it alone. Would you like to tell me what is on your heart?
One step: name one direction you want to turn from, say it to God in one sentence, and tell one trusted person.
src: Kingdom of God, Session 4: Entrance, Repentance, Consummation

items.q: Why did Jesus have to die?
a: Because we could not fix our own problem, and love would not leave us there.

Paul passed on what he received "as of first importance": that Christ died for our sins, was buried, and was raised on the third day, all according to the Scriptures (1 Corinthians 15:3–4). Colossians 2:13–15 says God forgave us all our trespasses, cancelled the record that stood against us, and nailed it to the cross, disarming the powers that held us. Isaiah 53:4–5 says He was pierced for our transgressions and by His wounds we are healed.
So the cross is not a tragedy that happened to Jesus. It is the price of your adoption (Galatians 4:4–5). And the empty tomb says it worked.
One step: this week, read Luke 23 and 24 in one sitting, and ask who in your life needs to hear that the grave is empty.
src: Wed Sep 09, Evidence for the Resurrection (1 Cor 15)

items.q: How can I be sure I am really a Christian?
a: Let me answer with what the text gives you, not with a feeling.

Romans 8:1: there is now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus. Titus 3:5: He saved us, not by works we did, but by His mercy, through the washing of rebirth and renewal by the Holy Spirit. Romans 8:16: the Spirit Himself bears witness with our spirit that we are God's children.
Notice where assurance sits. It sits on what Christ did, and the Spirit confirms it inside you. Your mood is a poor judge. A pilot trusts the instruments, not the feeling in the stomach.
Can I ask one thing? Is it doubt about whether God accepts you, or about something you have done?
One step: write Romans 8:1 on a card and read it out loud each morning for a week.
src: 30-Day Devotional (Day 10: No Condemnation
Day 15: The Miracle of the Spark)

items.q: Who am I in Christ?
a: You are someone God named before you did anything.
Think of Jesus at His baptism. The Father said, "This is My beloved Son," before Jesus had preached a sermon or healed one person (Matthew 3). Your name comes before your assignment.

In Christ, three things are settled: there is no condemnation for you (Romans 8:1). You are a son or daughter, an heir (Galatians 4:4–7). And you were bought with a price, so your body is a place where God lives (1 Corinthians 6:19–20).
*काम अघि नाम।* Name before work.
A leader who works to earn an identity gets shaken when the title or the applause is gone. A person who works from an identity can lose a position without losing themselves.
One step: tell God today, out loud, "You called me yours before I did anything." Then do one thing for someone else from that place.
src: 01 Identity: Name Before Assignment (Matthew 3) reel

items.q: I feel like God is disappointed in me. Is He?
a: I'm sorry you are carrying that. Can I ask one thing? Is it a sin you are ashamed of, or a feeling that nothing you do is enough?

Here is what the text says. Condemnation and conviction are different voices. Condemnation drives you away from God. Conviction draws you toward Him. Romans 8:1 says there is no condemnation for those in Christ. At His baptism, the Father called Jesus "beloved" before Jesus had done anything (Matthew 3:17). Your standing does not rise and fall with your best day.
God is not a disappointed boss. In Luke 15, the Father runs toward the son who left. Where He corrects you, it is the way a Father corrects a child He is not about to send away (Galatians 4:6–7).
One step: tell Him plainly what you did or feel. Then tell one trusted believer. Secrets weigh more than sins.
src: 30-Day Devotional (Day 10)

items.q: What does it mean that I am a son or daughter of God?
a: It means you are not a servant hoping to be tolerated. You are family.

Galatians 4:4–7: God sent His Son to redeem those under the law, so that we might receive adoption as sons. Because you are a son or daughter, God sent the Spirit of His Son into your heart, crying "Abba, Father." You are no longer a slave but a son, and if a son, then an heir through God.
Romans 8:14–17 adds that those led by the Spirit are God's children, and the Spirit bears witness with our spirit that we are His.
In Paul's picture, an infant heir looks no different from a servant until the father says the child is grown. The cross is the Father's announcement.
One step: this week, pray "Abba, Father" at the start of your prayer, and notice how it changes the first minute.
src: Sun Aug 23, From Slaves to Sons (Gal 4:4–7)
Sun Aug 30, Freedom for a Purpose

items.q: I keep failing at the same sin. Am I still loved?
a: Yes. You are still loved. Failing again does not turn God's love off.
Let me ask one thing: is this a struggle you have told anyone about?

Here is what the text says. Romans 6:4–11: you were buried with Christ and raised to walk in newness of life, so count yourself dead to sin and alive to God. That is not a mood. It is who you are in Him. Romans 8:1: no condemnation. And 1 John 1:9: if we confess our sins, He is faithful and just to forgive us and cleanse us.
Notice what Proverbs 24:16 says: the righteous fall seven times and rise again. The Bible does not say the righteous never stumble. The difference is that they refuse to stay down.
Freedom is also a community thing. Galatians 6:1–2 and James 5:16 point you toward a brother or sister who can carry this with you. Trying harder alone is the loneliest way to fight.
One step: this week, tell one trusted believer or a pastor. If you want, I can help you find the words.
Where to read more: Spiritual Fitness, Chapter 3 (pp. 38–39).
src: Book: Spiritual Fitness, Ch 3 (Prov 24:16)

items.q: How do I stop comparing myself to other people?
a: Comparison starts when we forget who set us where we are.
Galatians 6:4–5 tells each person to examine his own work, and then he can take pride in himself alone and not in comparison to someone else. Everyone carries their own load.

And in 1 Corinthians 12:18, Paul says God set each member in the body as He pleased. Set. The foot does not envy the hand, because the body is not whole without both. Your seat was chosen by God, not by a vote.
In the Father's house you are a son or daughter bought with a price (Galatians 4:4–7). Your worth was settled at the cross, not by the scoreboard.
One step: this week, when you notice yourself comparing, name one gift in the other person and thank God for it out loud. Then ask, "Whose hands can I help hold up today?"
src: Sun Oct 11, One Body, Many Parts
Wed Oct 07, One Body, Many Parts

items.q: What makes a good leader?
a: A good leader serves first and multiplies others.

Jesus put it plainly in Matthew 20:25–28. The rulers of the Gentiles lord it over people, but it will not be so among you. Whoever wants to be great must be your servant. Philippians 2:5–7 shows the pattern: Christ emptied Himself and took the form of a bond-servant.

Then there is multiplication. In 2 Timothy 2:2, Paul tells Timothy to entrust what he heard to faithful people who will teach others also. Four generations: Paul, Timothy, faithful people, others. A leader's real test is not how much they do, but how many leaders they leave behind.
One step: write down one person you could invest in for the next six months, and invite them for coffee this week.
*A towel, not a throne.*

items.q: How do I lead people who do not respect me?
a: That is a hard seat, and many leaders sit in it. Can I ask: do they disrespect you, or do they not yet know you?

Jesus separated position from influence. A title gives you authority on paper; people give you influence when they trust you (Matthew 20:25–28). So the answer is not to push harder. It is to serve well and keep showing up.
Two practical texts. A soft answer turns away wrath (Proverbs 15:1). And in John 4, Jesus connected with the woman at the well before He corrected her. Connection comes before correction.
Pray for those who are hard on you. Look for one thing you can do for each of them this week. People rarely follow a title, but they follow someone who helped them.
One step: pick the one person who respects you least, and do one quiet, concrete act of service for them.

items.q: What does servant leadership look like in real life?
a: Servant leadership looks like a towel, not a throne.
In Galatians 5:13, Paul says you were called to freedom, but do not use it as an opportunity for the flesh. Through love, serve one another. In John 13, Jesus knelt and washed the disciples' feet.
In real life it looks small. Showing up early to set up chairs. Listening before correcting. Sharing credit. Giving the platform to someone younger.
A servant leader is secure in who they are in Christ, so they do not need applause. A striver, by contrast, works from fear and the need for approval.
One step: this week, do one hidden job nobody will thank you for, and don't mention it.

items.q: How do I make a hard decision?
a: A hard decision deserves three companions: the Word, the Spirit, and wise people.

Psalm 119:105 says God's Word is a lamp to my feet. Acts 15:28 shows leaders saying, "It seemed good to the Holy Spirit and to us." Proverbs 15:22 says plans fail without counsel, but with many advisers they succeed. James 1:5 says that if you lack wisdom, ask God, who gives generously.

The men of Issachar understood the times and knew what to do (1 Chronicles 12:32). In Acts 16, Paul met closed doors and an open one, and the team reached its conclusion together. Discernment is rarely a solo act.
Can I ask one thing? What is the decision, and who have you talked to so far?
Your choices are real and they matter. We make them within God's care and sovereignty, so we choose with responsibility and with trust, not with fear.
One step: write the decision on a page, list what Scripture says, what you sense, and what two wise people say. Then wait a day before choosing.
Where to read more: Spiritual Fitness, Chapter 5 (p. 64 onward).
src: Book: Spiritual Fitness, Ch 5 The Architecture of Choice

items.q: How do I build self-discipline?
a: Self-discipline grows from a life you already have, not a life you are trying to earn.

Start with the order. Regeneration is the spark, the moment God gives life. Sanctification is the marathon. Paul uses the athlete's picture in 1 Corinthians 9:24–27, and in Philippians 2:12–13 he says to work out what God has worked in. God supplies the power; you supply the daily choices.

Then watch for drift. Nobody intends to drift, yet drift is the natural direction of an unanchored life. Small disciplines, repeated consistently, are what hold you steady. Give God your best energy first, not what is left at the end of a tired day (Proverbs 3:9). Every day brings many small decisions, and a few of them change the direction of a life. Deuteronomy 30:19 says choose life.

Your feelings will not vote for discipline at 5:00 in the morning. Your decisions will. So build the habit before you need the feeling, and tie it to something you already do, like praying over your family while the coffee brews.
Pick a shoreline, a clear mark you are heading toward, and fix your eyes on it (Habakkuk 2:2).
One step: choose one habit, one time, one place, for seven days. Tell one friend, so someone can ask you how it is going.
Where to read more: Spiritual Fitness, Chapter 1 (p. 2), Chapter 3 (pp. 37–38) and Chapter 5 (p. 64).

items.q: Who is the Holy Spirit and what does He do?
a: The Holy Spirit is God with you, not a force.
In John 14:16, Jesus calls Him another Helper, the Greek paraklētos: one called alongside to help. He is the third person of the Trinity, equal with the Father and the Son.

What does He do? He gives new life (Titus 3:5). He bears witness that you are God's child (Romans 8:16). He helps us pray when we have no words (Romans 8:26). He gives gifts to every believer for the common good (1 Corinthians 12:7). And at Pentecost, He filled the believers and empowered them to witness (Acts 2).
A simple way to say it: He walks alongside, lives inside, and works through you for others.
One step: this week, pray, "Holy Spirit, show me one person I can help." Then watch for them.
src: 52-Week Preaching Roadmap (W16 listing only)

items.q: What are spiritual gifts and how do I find mine?
a: Spiritual gifts are grace given to you for other people.

1 Corinthians 12:7: the manifestation of the Spirit is given to each one for the common good. Ephesians 4:7–13 says Christ gave gifts to equip the saints for the work of service. The Greek word is charisma, a grace gift, and symphoron means for the common good.

How do you find yours? Not by a test alone. Serve. Nehemiah 3 shows dozens of ordinary people each rebuilding the part of the wall near their own house. Gifts show up when you get busy. Then ask two people who know you, "Where do you see God using me?"
*Get ready, then get going.*
One step: this week, volunteer for one small task at church and ask someone to tell you what they noticed.
src: Sun Oct 18, Gifts for the Common Good: Get Ready, Then Get Going (Eph 4)

items.q: What is baptism in the Holy Spirit?
a: The baptism in the Holy Spirit is a gift Jesus gives to believers, for power to witness.

It is separate from being saved. At Pentecost the believers were filled with the Holy Spirit and spoke in other tongues as the Spirit gave them utterance (Acts 2:4). In Acts 19:6, when Paul laid hands on the Ephesian believers, the Spirit came and they spoke in tongues and prophesied. Jude 20 calls us to build ourselves up by praying in the Holy Spirit.

I hold, with the Assemblies of God, that speaking in tongues is the initial physical evidence of this baptism. Faithful believers outside our family read this differently, and I will not argue with them.
Can I ask: are you seeking this, or has someone told you that you need it to be saved? (You do not.)
One step: ask Jesus for it, in simple words, and talk to a pastor who can pray with you.
src: Sun Oct 04, Wind and Fire (Acts 2:1–4)

items.q: Why do I need church? Can't I follow Jesus on my own?
a: You can try, but you were not made to follow Jesus alone.

Before sin ever entered, God said it was not good for man to be alone (Genesis 2:18). In 1 Corinthians 12:18, Paul says God set each member in the body as He pleased. Set. You did not wander into your seat.

Think about your own body: a hand cut off is not free, it is just dead. In Exodus 17:12, even Moses needed a stone to sit on and two people to hold up his hands. The strongest leader in the Old Testament could not do it alone.
*Sit where God set you. Hold up someone's hands.* तपाईंको ठाउँ। अरूका हात।
Can I ask: what happened that made church hard for you?
One step: this week, go once, sit near someone new, and say, "I'm glad you're here."
Sources: Sunday sermon, Oct 11, 2026.
src: Sun Oct 11, One Body, Many Parts: Sit Where God Set You

items.q: What does it mean that the church is one body with many parts?
a: It means the church is one living body, and every part is needed.

Paul says it in 1 Corinthians 12:12–27: one body, many members. Notice how we get in. It is by one Spirit, not a membership class (12:13). Then he says the eye cannot say to the hand, "I don't need you," and the parts that seem weaker are necessary (12:21–22). If one suffers, all suffer; if one is honored, all rejoice (12:26).
At the Lord's table, there is one loaf. Many people, one body (1 Corinthians 10:17). Every time you take the bread, you are saying, "I belong to these people."
The body is not whole without you.
One step: this week, find one person who seems "weak" or overlooked in your church and tell them how they help the body.
src: Wed Oct 07, One Body, Many Parts

items.q: I am stressed and anxious all the time. What does the Bible say?
a: That sounds exhausting, and I'm glad you said it. Can I ask: is it worse at night, or all day?

Scripture does not mock anxiety. When Elijah was worn out after Mount Carmel and said, "Enough, Lord," God's first answer was not a sermon. It was "Arise, eat" (1 Kings 19). *उठ, खाऊ।* God restores before He redirects. Rest, food and His presence come first.
Then Scripture gives the invitation: cast all your anxiety on Him, because He cares for you (1 Peter 5:7), and bring everything to Him in prayer with thanksgiving (Philippians 4:6–7).
If the anxiety is constant, see a doctor or counselor too. That is wisdom, not weak faith.
One step: tonight, sleep, eat something, and tell one trusted person how heavy it feels.
src: 03 Suffering: The Broom Tree Principle (1 Kings 19) reel

items.q: How should I think about money and giving?
a: Think of money as a tool, and watch your heart.

A sermon I preached on October 18 shows it: 1 Timothy 6:6–10 says godliness with contentment is great gain. It is not that money is bad. It is that the desire to get rich is a trap, and what it costs you is your faith. Contentment in God is the real wealth. *Enough* is a gift.

On giving: Genesis 12:2 says "be a blessing." God makes grace abound to you so that you have enough for every good deed (2 Corinthians 9:8). Joseph stored in the good years so a nation could eat in the hard ones (Genesis 41). Giving and saving both serve people.

I won't promise that giving makes you rich. Scripture doesn't. Success is not wrong, and God often blesses faithful stewardship. The danger is making success the destination. Success asks what I can accomplish. Significance asks who benefits because I lived.
One step: write down what "enough" would be for you this year, and one person or ministry you will bless from it.
Where to read more: Spiritual Fitness, Chapter 8 (pp. 114–115).

items.q: My marriage is struggling. Where do I start?
a: I'm sorry. That is a painful place to be. Can I ask one thing first? Are you safe at home?
If there is any fear or harm, please reach out to a trusted pastor, a domestic violence hotline, or emergency services before anything else.

If it is conflict and drift, start small. Ephesians 4:15 says speak the truth in love. A "family altar" can help: one short, regular time to pray and read together, even five minutes. Your small group guide builds one for families.
Be careful with "I'll take 100% ownership." Take your share, but do not carry the whole load for both of you.
My library has little on marriage, so I'll stay brief. A pastor or a licensed marriage counselor can walk with you in ways I cannot.
One step: ask your spouse for a ten-minute talk this week, with no phones, and begin with one thing you appreciate.
src: Spiritual Fitness: 6-Week Small Group & Family Altar Guide
8-Week Discipleship Curriculum

items.q: How do I raise my children in the faith?
a: Start at home, in small, regular ways.

Deuteronomy 6 is the pattern: love God yourself first, then talk about His words when you sit, walk, lie down and rise. Psalm 78:1–8 tells parents to tell the next generation the praiseworthy deeds of the Lord so each generation sets its hope in God.
Your book's picture: a thermostat sets the temperature of the room; a thermometer just reads it. Parents set the spiritual climate. Children copy what we are more than what we say.
Try a weekly family altar: one Bible story, one question at the table, one short prayer, and a blessing laid on each child's head. Keep it short and warm.
Can I ask: how old are your children?
One step: choose one night this week, 10 minutes, one story, one prayer. Start there.
src: Spiritual Fitness: Family Altar & Household Worship Companion

items.q: I am lonely and far from home. How do I keep going?
a: That is a heavy kind of lonely, and I'm glad you said it.
Look at what God did with scattered people in Acts 11:19–21. Believers who were driven out went everywhere sharing the good news, and a church grew in Antioch. Scattered can become sown.
Loneliness was never God's idea. He said, "It is not good for man to be alone" (Genesis 2:18). He puts the lonely in families (Psalm 68:6).
Can I ask: do you have a church or a small group near you?
One step: this week, find one table. A fellowship meal, a prayer group, a phone call to someone from home. Then be the one who notices the lonely person in the room and invites them to sit with you.
Where to read more: Spiritual Fitness, Chapter 6 (p. 91).

items.q: Do I have to speak in tongues to be saved?
a: No. Speaking in tongues is not required to be saved.
Salvation is by grace through faith in Christ. Ephesians 2:8–9. If you have trusted Jesus, you are saved.

The baptism in the Holy Spirit is a separate gift for power to witness. In Acts 2:4 and Acts 19:6, believers spoke in tongues when the Spirit came. I teach, as the Assemblies of God does, that tongues is the initial physical evidence of that baptism. Faithful believers in other traditions see it differently, and I won't argue with them. Unity matters more than winning (Ephesians 4).
Can I ask: has someone made you feel less saved without it?
If so, I'm sorry. You are not less loved.
One step: if you're curious, read Acts 2 and ask Jesus for what He has for you. No pressure.
src: Sun Oct 04, Wind and Fire (Acts 2:1–4)
Wed Sep 30, Pentecost

items.q: Is my child's illness my fault?
a: No. I'm so sorry you're carrying this question.
Can I ask: what's happening with your child?

Scripture is clear on one thing: sickness is not a verdict on a parent. In John 9:1–3, the disciples asked whose sin caused a man's blindness. Jesus said it was neither his nor his parents'. I won't promise a particular outcome, and I won't blame you.

Please stay close to the child's doctors. Praying and seeing a doctor go together. James 5:14–15 tells us to call for the elders to pray and anoint with oil. Call your pastor too, and let your church carry meals, rides and prayer.
Parents grieve and worry. That is love.
One step: ask one person today to take one specific thing off your plate.
If you want, I can write a short prayer for you and your child.

items.q: Will God make me rich if I give?
a: No. Scripture doesn't promise that giving makes you rich, and I won't either.
1 Timothy 6:6–10 warns the opposite: the desire to get rich is a trap, and it costs people their faith. Godliness with contentment is the real gain. *Enough* is the gift.

What Scripture does say is that God provides for those who give. In 2 Corinthians 9:8, God is able to make all grace abound to you so that, having all sufficiency, you may have an abundance for every good deed. Notice: sufficiency for good deeds, not luxury for yourself.
Give because you were given to. Give with joy, quietly, and never to bargain with God.
Can I ask what's behind the question? Are you worried about money?
One step: choose one amount to give this month because you are grateful, not to get anything back.
src: Enough Is the Real Wealth (1 Tim 6:6–10)

items.q: My Hindu family says I have betrayed them. What do I do?
a: I'm sorry. That is a painful wound, being told you have betrayed your own people. Can I ask one thing? Are you safe, and are they treating you well?
If there is threat or violence, please reach out to a trusted pastor, a safe adult, or local help first.

If it is hurt feelings, here is what the text says. Honor your father and mother (Exodus 20:12; Ephesians 6:2). Following Jesus does not cancel your love for your family. Peter says to give a reason for your hope, with gentleness and respect (1 Peter 3:15). Don't speak harshly about their faith. They are not your enemies.
Keep showing love by showing up: call, serve, and eat with them. Many families change their minds slowly, watching a life that matches the words.
One step: this week, do one small kindness for your family, without a sermon.
src: Sun Oct 11, One Body, Many Parts (Hindu home, family baptism)
Wed Oct 21, The Living Temple

items.q: I'm angry at my pastor.
a: That's a hard thing to carry about someone you may love. Can I ask: did something happen, or has it been building?
First, you are allowed to be hurt. Pastors are people. Don't bury it.

Then, here is what the text says. If someone has sinned against you, go to him privately (Matthew 18:15). Speak the truth in love (Ephesians 4:15). Connection comes before correction: Jesus sat with the woman at the well before He said a hard word (John 4). Pray before you talk.
If the issue is abuse or misuse of power, you don't need to stay quiet. Talk to another trusted leader or a denominational office, and take someone with you.
An unforgiving heart hurts you most (Ephesians 4:31–32).
One step: this week, write what you'd say, then pray over it. Ask for a calm conversation, not a confrontation.
src: 04 Wisdom: The Unoffendable Leader (Prov 19
Matthew 18:15)
04 Wisdom: Connection Precedes Correction (John 4)

items.q: Is it wrong to have doubts?
a: No. Doubt is not the opposite of faith. It's often faith asking questions.

Mark 9:24: a father cried, "I do believe; help my unbelief!" and Jesus helped him. Thomas wanted to touch the wounds, and Jesus came to him and showed him (John 20:24–29). Jude 22 says to have mercy on those who doubt.
The Resurrection was not asked to be believed blind. Paul lists the witnesses (1 Corinthians 15:1–8). Honest questions have a place.

Where doubt goes wrong is when it leads to cold isolation and pulls you away from the body of believers. Handled honestly, in community, a search for the truth can lead to a deeper foundation. So don't run from your hardest questions. Change their direction: turn each doubt into a prayer, "Lord, I believe; help my unbelief," and keep studying.
Can I ask: what are you doubting? God, the Bible, or whether He cares about you?
One step: write your biggest question down this week, pray it back to God, and take it to a pastor or a mature friend.
Where to read more: Spiritual Fitness, Chapter 5 (pp. 76–77).

items.q: What does the Bible say about divorce?
a: I'm sorry. Whatever brought you to this question, it's heavy. Can I ask one thing first? Are you safe?
If there is abuse, fear, or violence, please reach out to a trusted pastor or local help before anything else. You're not required to stay in danger.

My library does not teach on divorce, so I won't answer it as if it did. I can say that Scripture takes marriage seriously (Matthew 19:3–9) and also speaks to the grief and brokenness around it (1 Corinthians 7:10–15). Faithful believers read these passages with different emphases.
This is a conversation for a pastor and, where needed, a licensed counselor. I'd rather send you to a real person who can listen than give you a verdict.
One step: call your pastor this week and ask for an hour. If you'd like, I can help you write what to say.

items.q: Why wasn't I healed? Did I not have enough faith?
a: I'm sorry. I won't tell you that. Scripture doesn't blame sick people for lacking faith. Would you like to tell me what you've been going through?

Here is what the text shows. We believe God heals. We pray, and we anoint with oil (James 5:14–15). And Scripture also shows people who were not healed right away. Paul asked three times about his thorn and heard, "My grace is sufficient for you" (2 Corinthians 12:7–10). Epaphroditus was sick almost to death, and God had mercy (Philippians 2:25–27). Paul left Trophimus sick at Miletus (2 Timothy 4:20).
You are not behind, and you are not a failure. You were never meant to wait alone.
One step: talk with your doctor and with a pastor you trust. If you'd like, I can write a short prayer for you.
src: Wed Aug 26, The Power of Weakness (2 Cor 12:7–10)
Kingdom Leadership: Divine Healing Part 2

items.q: My mother is very sick and I'm worn out. I don't know how to pray.
a: I'm so sorry. That's a heavy load, and being tired doesn't mean you're failing. Would it help if I told you a little about what Scripture says to someone in your place, or would you rather tell me about her first?

When you don't have words, Romans 8:26 says the Spirit helps us in our weakness. In Exodus 17:12, Moses' hands grew heavy, and Aaron and Hur held them up. The greatest leader in the Old Testament needed a seat and two people standing beside him. You were not made to hold this alone.
One step: this week, ask one person to carry one specific thing, such as a meal, a ride, or an hour sitting with your mother.

If you'd like, here is a short prayer you can pray with me: "Father, I'm tired. Hold up my arms, and send me someone who will stand beside me. Be near my mother. Amen." If you ever feel hopeless or unsafe, please call someone you trust or a crisis line right now, and talk with your pastor.
src: Sun Oct 11, One Body, Many Parts (Exodus 17:8–13)
Wed Aug 26, The Power of Weakness

items.q: Does God heal today?
a: Yes. I believe God heals today, and Scripture gives us good reason.

Isaiah 53:4–5: by His wounds we are healed. In Mark 16:17–18, Jesus says signs will follow those who believe, including laying hands on the sick. James 5:14–15 tells the sick to call the elders, who pray and anoint with oil.
Healing is one of the great works of Jesus, and the Assemblies of God counts divine healing among its four cardinal doctrines.

I also hold the other half. Scripture shows faithful people who were not healed right away: Paul's thorn (2 Corinthians 12:7–10), Epaphroditus (Philippians 2:25–27), Trophimus (2 Timothy 4:20). I will never say a sick person lacks faith, and I won't promise a particular result.
Can I ask: are you asking for yourself or for someone you love?
One step: ask a pastor to pray and anoint with oil, and keep seeing your doctor.
src: Kingdom Leadership: Divine Healing Parts 1–4

items.q: Is the thorn in the flesh a sickness?
a: Paul's own words are "a messenger of Satan to torment me" (2 Corinthians 12:7). I hold that the thorn was a messenger, not an illness.

Look at how "thorn" is used in the Old Testament. It means opposing people and persecution: Numbers 33:55, Joshua 23:13, Judges 2:3, Ezekiel 28:24. So the picture is one of resistance and opposition, which fits Paul's life of beatings and prison.

Whichever way you read it, the center of the passage is the same. Paul asked three times. The answer was grace, not removal: "My grace is sufficient for you, for power is perfected in weakness" (2 Corinthians 12:8–9). Faithful believers differ on the thorn's identity, and I won't make this a fight.
One step: if you are carrying your own thorn, read 2 Corinthians 12:7–10 slowly and tell God what you'd ask three times.
src: Wed Aug 26, The Power of Weakness (2 Cor 12:7–10)

items.q: How do I become a Christian?
a: Becoming a Christian starts with trusting Jesus, not with being good enough first.

Scripture says all of us have fallen short (Romans 3:23), and that salvation is a gift of grace through faith, not something we earn (Ephesians 2:8-9). Romans 10:9-10 says that if you confess Jesus as Lord and believe God raised Him from the dead, you will be saved. John 1:12 says everyone who receives Him becomes a child of God.

You can say it to God in your own words: that you are sorry, that you believe Jesus died and rose for you, and that you want to follow Him. God has offered this to everyone (John 3:16-18), and the choice is yours.
One step: tell a pastor or a believer you trust today, and ask to be baptized and to join a church family.
If you want, I can help you put your prayer into words.

items.q: How do I forgive someone who hurt me?
a: I'm sorry you were hurt. That pain is real, and forgiving does not mean pretending it did not happen.

Forgiving is a decision to release the debt, because God released ours (Ephesians 4:32; Colossians 3:13). Jesus asked the Father to forgive the people who crucified Him (Luke 23:34). When Peter asked how many times, Jesus answered with a number meant to say, don't keep count (Matthew 18:21-22).

Forgiving is not the same as trusting the person again, and it does not cancel wise boundaries. If you are in danger, please get safe and talk with a pastor or counselor first. Romans 12:17-19 reminds us we leave justice to God.
Can I ask: is this a recent wound, or an old one?
One step: write the person's name, tell God you release them, and ask Him for the strength to mean it. You may need to do it more than once.

items.q: How do I forgive myself?
a: Start with this: if you have confessed it to God, He has already forgiven you.

1 John 1:9 says that if we confess our sins, He is faithful and righteous to forgive us and cleanse us. Romans 8:1 says there is now no condemnation for those in Christ Jesus. Psalm 103:12 says He removes our sins as far as the east is from the west.
Carrying guilt after God has forgiven is not humility. It is believing your verdict over His. Real sorrow leads you back to Him and to change, and shame pushes you away.
Can I ask: is there something you still need to make right with another person?
One step: say out loud, "God has forgiven me," then do the next right thing, and tell one trusted person.

items.q: How do I pray?
a: You do not need special words. Prayer is talking with your Father.

The disciples asked Jesus to teach them to pray (Luke 11:1), and He gave them the Lord's Prayer (Matthew 6:9-13). It begins with who God is, then asks for daily needs, forgiveness and protection. Philippians 4:6 says to bring everything to God with thanksgiving. When we do not know what to say, the Spirit helps us in our weakness (Romans 8:26).
A simple pattern: thank Him, tell Him what is on your heart, ask for what you need, listen, and say amen. Short and honest is enough.
One step: pick one time and one place tomorrow, and pray for five minutes. Start with the Lord's Prayer and then say what is on your heart.

items.q: What is fasting and should I do it?
a: Fasting is going without food, or something else, for a time to give your attention to God.

Jesus said "when you fast," not "if" (Matthew 6:16-18), and told us to do it quietly, not to be noticed. The early church fasted while seeking God's direction (Acts 13:2-3). Isaiah 58:6 shows God cares about the heart: fasting that leads to justice and care for others.
It is not a way to force God's hand. It is a way to make room for Him.

If you have a medical condition, take medication, are pregnant, or are very young or elderly, please talk with a doctor first. You can fast from something else, like social media, if food is not safe for you.
One step: start small. Skip one meal this week and spend that time in prayer and Scripture.

items.q: I lost someone I love. How do I get through this?
a: I'm so sorry. Grief is the price of love, and there is no wrong way to cry.

Jesus wept at the tomb of His friend (John 11:35), so tears are not a lack of faith. Psalm 34:18 says the Lord is near to the brokenhearted. Matthew 5:4 says those who mourn will be comforted. For those who belong to Jesus, Paul says we do not grieve like those who have no hope (1 Thessalonians 4:13).
Let people sit with you. Let them bring food. You do not have to be strong for anyone tonight.
Can I ask: who was the person you lost?

One step: tell one person today how you are really doing, and accept one practical help. If the grief feels like too much, please talk with your pastor or a counselor, and call or text 988 in the US if you feel unsafe.

items.q: I am afraid all the time. What does God say about fear?
a: Fear is exhausting, and I'm glad you said it. You are not weak for feeling it.

God speaks into fear again and again. Isaiah 41:10 says do not fear, for He is with you; He will strengthen you and help you. 2 Timothy 1:7 says God did not give us a spirit of fear but of power, love and self-control. The psalmist says, "When I am afraid, I will put my trust in You" (Psalm 56:3), which means fear and trust can be in the same heart at the same time.
If the fear is constant, please see a doctor or counselor as well. That is wisdom, not a lack of faith.
Can I ask: what is the fear about?
One step: tonight, pray one sentence out loud, "God, I am afraid, and I trust You," and tell one person how heavy it feels.

items.q: I feel hopeless. Where is God in this?
a: I'm glad you told me. I'm sorry it feels this heavy. Please do not carry this alone.

Scripture does not hide from dark days. The psalmist asks his own soul, "Why are you in despair?" and then tells it to hope in God (Psalm 42:5). Elijah was so worn out he asked to die, and God's first move was care: sleep, food, and His quiet presence (1 Kings 19).
If you are thinking of ending your life, or you are in danger, call or text 988 in the US, or call your local emergency number right now. Please also tell a pastor, a family member or a friend today.
Hopelessness often needs a doctor or counselor as well as prayer. That is not weak faith.
One step: reach one real person today and tell them exactly what you told me.

items.q: How do I find hope in suffering?
a: Suffering is real, and the Bible does not rush past it.

Paul says suffering produces endurance, endurance character, and character hope, and the hope does not disappoint because God's love has been poured into our hearts (Romans 5:3-5). James 1:2-4 says testing builds steadiness. 2 Corinthians 4:16-18 says our troubles are light and temporary compared with what is coming. Romans 8:28 says God works in all things for the good of those who love Him. It does not say all things are good.
God is not far from you in it. Psalm 23 says even in the valley of the shadow, He is with us.
Can I ask: what are you facing right now?
One step: write down one thing God has carried you through before, and thank Him for it. Then ask one person to walk beside you this week.

items.q: I am exhausted and burned out. What should I do?
a: It sounds like you have given a lot. Being tired is not a failure of faith.

Jesus said, "Come to Me, all who are weary and heavy-laden, and I will give you rest" (Matthew 11:28). He told His busy disciples to come away and rest (Mark 6:31). God built rest into the week (Exodus 20:8-11). Elijah, after a great victory, was worn out, and God's answer was "Arise, eat" (1 Kings 19).
Rest is part of obeying God. If the exhaustion has lasted weeks, please see a doctor and talk with your pastor.
One step: choose one thing to stop doing this week and protect one real day of rest.

items.q: How do I wait on God when nothing is changing?
a: Waiting is one of the hardest kinds of faith, and I'm sorry you are in it.

Psalm 27:14 says to wait for the Lord, be strong, and let your heart take courage. Isaiah 40:31 says those who wait for the Lord will renew their strength. Habakkuk 2:3 says the vision waits for its appointed time, and though it tarries, wait for it.
Waiting is not doing nothing. It is staying faithful while God works in ways you cannot see yet. Keep praying, keep obeying what you already know, and keep your community close.

items.q: How do I read the Bible so it actually makes sense?
a: Start small, and start with Jesus.

2 Timothy 3:16-17 says Scripture is given by God to teach, correct and equip us. Psalm 119:105 says it is a lamp to my feet. In Acts 17:11, the Bereans received the message eagerly and checked the Scriptures daily.
A simple way: begin with the Gospel of John, read one short section a day, and ask three questions. What does it say? What does it show me about God? What is one thing I will do about it?
Read a whole paragraph, not one verse alone. Ask a pastor when something is confusing, and read with others if you can.
One step: tonight, read John 1 and write one sentence about what you noticed.

items.q: How do I know God's will for my life?
a: Start by trusting Him, because He is good and He knows the way.

Proverbs 3:5-6 says to trust in the Lord with all your heart, not lean on your own understanding, and He will make your paths straight. Psalm 119:105 says His word lights the way. Romans 12:2 says a renewed mind is how we test and approve what God's will is. James 1:5 says if anyone lacks wisdom, ask God, who gives generously. Proverbs 11:14 says there is safety in many counselors.
God's will is usually found in a few things together: Scripture, prayer, wise people, and the next faithful step. He may not show you the whole road.

items.q: How do I find my calling and purpose?
a: Your purpose starts with who you are in Christ, not with a job title.

Ephesians 2:10 says we are God's workmanship, created in Christ Jesus for good works that God prepared beforehand. 1 Corinthians 12 says every member of the body is needed. Colossians 3:23 says whatever you do, work at it with all your heart as for the Lord.
Often calling shows up where your gifts, your care for people, and a real need meet. It grows as you serve, not only as you think about it.

items.q: How do I resist temptation?

1 Corinthians 10:13 says no temptation has overtaken you except what is common to people, and God is faithful and will provide a way out. items.q: How do I stay grateful when life is hard?
a: Gratitude does not deny the hard things. It looks for God's hand in them.

1 Thessalonians 5:18 says to give thanks in all circumstances. Psalm 100 invites us to enter His gates with thanksgiving. In Luke 17:11-19, ten lepers were healed, but only one came back to thank Jesus.
Thankfulness changes what we notice. Start with small things: a meal, a friend, a morning.

items.q: How do I stay honest and keep my integrity at work?

items.q: How do I become humble without being a doormat?
a: Humility is not thinking less of yourself. It is thinking of yourself less.

Philippians 2:3-8 says to count others more significant, and shows Jesus, who emptied Himself and took the form of a servant. James 4:6 says God opposes the proud and gives grace to the humble. Micah 6:8 says to walk humbly with your God.
Jesus was never a doormat. He was humble and also spoke the truth. Humble people know who they are in Christ, so they do not need applause.

items.q: I was hurt by people in the church. Should I give up on church?
a: I'm sorry. Being hurt by God's people is one of the deepest hurts, and it deserves to be taken seriously.

The church is made of imperfect people, and the Bible says so. Jesus gave a path for when someone wrongs you: go to them privately first (Matthew 18:15). Paul says, as far as it depends on you, live at peace with everyone (Romans 12:18). Hebrews 10:24-25 says not to give up meeting together, because we need each other.
If you were abused or harmed by a leader, that is not your fault, and you do not owe that person access to you. Please talk with a pastor or counselor you trust.
Can I ask: what happened?
One step: tell one safe person what happened, and consider visiting a church or small group where you can be loved again.

items.q: How do we handle conflict in the church?
a: Conflict is normal in a family. How we handle it shows who we belong to.

Jesus said to go to the person privately first, then take one or two others, and involve the church last (Matthew 18:15-17). Ephesians 4:1-3 says to walk worthy of your calling, with humility and gentleness, patient with one another, working to keep the unity of the Spirit. Philippians 2:2 says to be of one mind in love.
Talk to the person, not about the person. Assume the best, ask questions, and aim for restoring the relationship, not winning.
One step: if you have a grievance, pray for that person by name this week, then go to them in private.

items.q: How do I share my faith with friends and family?
a: You do not need to be a preacher. You need to be a friend whose life matches what you say.

1 Peter 3:15 says to always be ready to give a reason for your hope, with gentleness and respect. Colossians 4:5-6 says to be wise toward outsiders, with speech full of grace. Jesus told His followers to go and make disciples (Matthew 28:19-20). When Philip met Nathanael, he said, "Come and see" (John 1:46).
Listen first. Ask questions. Share how Jesus has changed your life, and invite them to church, a meal or a conversation. Don't argue. Pray for them by name.

items.q: What is baptism and do I need it?
a: Baptism is a public step that says, "I belong to Jesus."

In Acts 8:36-38, the Ethiopian believed and was baptized right away. Baptism does not save us. Grace through faith does (Ephesians 2:8-9). It is the first step of obedience after you believe.
Talk with your pastor about being baptized. It is a celebration with the church family.

items.q: What is communion and why do we take it?
a: Communion is a meal of remembering. We remember what Jesus did for us.

On the night He was betrayed, Jesus broke bread and said to do this in remembrance of Him (Luke 22:19; 1 Corinthians 11:23-26). In 1 Corinthians 10:16-17, Paul says the one loaf shows we are one body. Paul also says to examine ourselves and not take it carelessly (1 Corinthians 11:27-29), meaning with honesty and care for each other.
It is a time to thank Jesus, to confess where you need to, and to remember that you belong to these people.
One step: the next time we take communion, spend a quiet minute before it, thanking Jesus and making peace with anyone you need to.

items.q: How do I talk to my teenager about faith?

Ask real questions. Admit your own struggles. Let them see you pray and serve. Pray for them by name. Give them space to ask hard questions.

items.q: How do I handle peer pressure as a teenager?
